newsitem.title: UK: Core European bonds may offer safe haven in downturn.
newsitem.headline: Core European bonds may offer safe haven in downturn.

text.p: World bonds face a bumpy downward ride in the next few months, but German and other core European bond markets offer the most stability for international investors, analysts said on Monday.
"Europe will outperform on the way down, with the short end of core Europe remaining fairly well underpinned," said Philip Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC Futures in London.
U.S. and European bonds fell on Friday after strong U.S. retail sales and producer price data caught investors by surprise and fuelled expectations of a May rise in U.S. interest rates.
"The majority of the market is expecting the Fed (U.S. Federal Reserve) to go again," said Mark Fox, chief European strategist, fixed income, at Lehman Brothers in London.
The federal funds target rate was raised to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent in March, the first U.S. rate rise in nearly 14 months.
The yield on the U.S. 30-year bond, which was at 7.18 percent at 1030 GMT, will soon leave the seven percent threshold behind, analysts said.
"There might be room for a small correction in the early part of this week, but the overall tone is down," said Tyson. "The long bond yield will move up to 7.25 to 7.30 percent."

But a more attractive fundamental picture in Germany would allow the yield spread between 10-year U.S. Treasuries and German Bunds to widen, analysts said. Yield differentials measure the relative risk between two countries' government debt.
"Bunds will push lower but outperform further, and the spread can go to 120 basis points," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International in London.
The 10-year T-note/Bund spread was at 115 basis points at 1030 GMT.
A benign inflation picture and stable interest rate environment were supporting the shorter end of the German yield curve in particular, analysts said.
"German rates will remain on hold for this year and well into next year," said Tyson. "Core European yield curves will retain a fairly steep stance."
But on a 12-month basis, the 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread could narrow to 50 basis points, analysts said.
"We will see economic divergence the other way around, with the U.S. economy slowing, and the German economy picking up," said Brickman.
In contrast to other analysts, Lehman's Fox did not expect Germany to outpace the United States over the next few months.
"European bond markets have shown a fairly poor ability to resist the downward pressures of the U.S.. Europe may outperform only slightly."
Germany and core Europe still looked attractive compared with peripheral Europe, analysts said.
"Long end (peripheral) spreads will ebb and flow with EMU (European economic and monetary union) sentiment," said Teis Knutsen, international economist at First Chicago in London.
EMU uncertainty counteracted more positive expectations of interest rate cuts in Spain and Italy, analysts said.

The Bank of Spain is expected to cut its 5.75 percent key money market rate by at least 25 basis points on Tuesday, while markets are looking for an Italian rate cut after the next batch of inflation data.
"Two weeks ago we became neutral on the peripherals versus core Europe and we will remain so," said Fox. "We were negative on the peripherals from December until then."
